newsitem.title: UK: Britain's trade deficit shrinks despite strong pound.
newsitem.headline: Britain's trade deficit shrinks despite strong pound.

text.p: Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the world shrank to 845 million pounds ($1.4 billion) in December, according to official figures released Wednesday, undercutting forecasts and casting doubt on how much the strong pound sterling is hurting exporters.

The Office for National Statistics said Britain's trade gap narrowed from more than 1 billion pounds ($1.63 billion) in November. Economists had forecast a global deficit of about 1.1 billion ($1.8 billion).
Treasury Economic Secretary Angela Knight said Britain's trade performance was as strong as it had been in a decade.
"The competitive strength of British industry shines through today's trade figures," she said in a statement.

Britain's trade shortfall with non-European Union countries also fell to 398 million pounds ($652.5 million) in January, well under December's 640 million ($1.05 billion) gap and economist forecasts for a deficit of around 750 million ($1.23 billion) pounds.
Ciaran Barr, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the trade figures were much better than expected and suggested the pound had yet to really hit exports.
Economists said, however, that Britain's trade could not withstand the pressure applied by the pound forever, unless the currency began falling soon.

Sterling has rocketed about 16 percent in little more than six months, as measured against a basket of major currencies. A strong pound has the effect of cutting import prices but pushing those for exports higher.
Britain exported goods and services worth 13.987 billion pounds ($22.9 billion) in December, up from 13.754 billion ($22.5 billion) the month before.
"Exports were better than expected in both the global and non-EU figures," Barr said. "It may be several months until we can identify the impact of sterling strength feeding through."
Exports to non-European Union countries totalled 6.36 billion pounds ($10.4 billion) in January, much higher than the 5.97 billion ($9.8 billion) worth shipped in December.
